title_en: Supreme People's Court Releases Typical Cases of Administrative Disputes over Work-Related Injury Insurance
keywords_en: Contract for Work; Arbitration; Work-Related Injury; Administrative Dispute over Work-Related Injury Insurance (Court Issued)
full_text_en:
Supreme People's Court

Publishes Typical Cases on Administrative Disputes over Work-related Injury Insurance

Case 1    Zhang Chengbing v. Shanghai Songjiang District Human Resources and Social Security Bureau — administrative dispute over work-related injury identification

— Where an employing unit subcontracts or contracts out contracted business to an organization or individual without employing entity qualifications in violation of laws or regulations, and an employee hired by such organization or individual suffers work-related injury or death, the employing unit shall be the entity assuming responsibility for work-related injury insurance.

Basic Facts

Nantong Liujian Company was the contractor of the A7 factory building project of Guoji Electronics (Shanghai) Co., Ltd. It subcontracts the painting work to an individual, Li Moumou, in the form of a "Paint Contract," stipulating that the personnel employed by Li Moumou shall be subject to the management of Nantong Liujian Company. Li Moumou then subcontracts part of the painting work to another individual, Wang Moumou, who hired Zhang Chengbing to carry out the painting work. Neither Li Moumou nor Wang Moumou had the qualification of an employing entity, nor the corresponding qualifications for undertaking the painting work. On March 10, 2008, Zhang Chengbing was accidentally injured while performing painting work. On November 10, the Songjiang District Labor Arbitration Committee ruled that a labor relationship existed between Zhang Chengbing and Nantong Liujian Company, but the ruling was not served on Nantong Liujian Company. On December 29, Zhang Chengbing filed an application for work-related injury identification, submitting the labor arbitration ruling. After accepting the case and conducting an investigation, the Shanghai Songjiang District Human Resources and Social Security Bureau found that Zhang Chengbing's injury met the conditions for work-related injury identification, and that Nantong Liujian Company, after being notified, failed to present evidence regarding whether Zhang Chengbing's injury should be identified as a work-related injury. Therefore, on February 19, 2009, the Shanghai Songjiang District Human Resources and Social Security Bureau determined that Zhang Chengbing's injury was a work-related injury. Nantong Liujian Company refused to accept this determination and, after unsuccessful administrative reconsideration, filed a lawsuit requesting the revocation of the work-related injury identification made by the Shanghai Songjiang District Human Resources and Social Security Bureau.

Judgment

After trial at first instance by the Songjiang District People's Court of Shanghai and at second instance by the Shanghai No. 1 Intermediate People's Court, the court held that, according to Article 4 of the Ministry of Labor and Social Security Notice No. 12 (2005) on Relevant Issues Concerning the Establishment of Labor Relations, when an employing unit in the construction or mining industry contracts out a project (or business) or operational rights to an organization or individual without employing entity qualifications, the contractor with employing entity qualifications shall bear the employing entity responsibility for the workers hired by such organization or individual. In this case, Nantong Liujian Company, as a construction unit, contracted out the painting work to an individual, Li Moumou, who lacked employing entity qualifications, with a stipulation that the personnel employed by Li Moumou should be subject to the management of Nantong Liujian Company. Subsequently, Li Moumou further subcontracts part of the painting work to Wang Moumou, who hired the appellant, Zhang Chengbing, to perform the painting work. The Shanghai Songjiang District Human Resources and Social Security Bureau's determination that a labor relationship existed between the appellant and the appellee based on the above provisions and facts was justified. According to the provisions of the Regulations on Work-related Injury Insurance, Zhang Chengbing's accidental injury while performing painting work in the factory building project contracted by Jiangsu Nantong Liujian Construction Group Co., Ltd. fell within the scope of work-related injury identification. Accordingly, the court upheld the specific administrative act of the Shanghai Songjiang District Human Resources and Social Security Bureau in making the challenged work-related injury identification.

Case 2    Sun Lixing v. Tianjin New Technology Industrial Park Labor Bureau — administrative dispute over work-related injury identification

— The determination of work-related cause and work premises should consider whether it is related to the performance of work duties and whether the injury occurred within a reasonable area.

Basic Facts

Sun Lixing was an employee of Zhongli Company. On the morning of June 10, 2003, he was assigned by the person in charge of Zhongli Company to pick up someone at the Beijing airport. He went downstairs from the eighth floor of the International Business Center (hereinafter referred to as the Business Center) in Huayuan Industrial Park, Nankai District, Tianjin, where Zhongli Company was located, intending to drive a car in the courtyard of the Business Center. When he reached the steps at the first-floor entrance, Sun Lixing slipped and fell from four steps to the ground. He was diagnosed at the hospital with cervical spinal cord hyperextension injury with cervical nerve root traction injury, upper lip contusion and laceration, abrasion of the left arm, and skin abrasion of the left leg. Sun Lixing applied to the Park Labor Bureau for work-related injury identification. On March 5, 2004, the Park Labor Bureau issued a "Decision on Work-related Injury Identification," stating that there was no evidence to show that Sun Lixing's fall injury occurred in the workplace or was caused by work-related reasons, and decided not to identify it as a work-related injury.

Judgment

After trial at first instance by the Tianjin No. 1 Intermediate People's Court and at second instance by the Tianjin High People's Court, the court held that the focal issue in this case was whether the location where Sun Lixing fell constituted a workplace and whether it was work-related. The Regulations on Work-related Injury Insurance provide that an employee who suffers an accident injury during working hours and at the workplace due to work-related reasons shall be identified as having a work-related injury. The term "workplace" in this provision refers to the place where an employee engages in professional activities. In the case of multiple workplaces, it should also include the necessary areas through which the employee travels between the multiple workplaces. In this case, the office of Zhongli Company on the eighth floor of the Business Center was Sun Lixing's workplace, and the car he needed to drive to complete the work task of picking someone up at the airport was another workplace of his. The car was parked outside the first-floor entrance of the Business Center. To complete the task of driving the car, Sun Lixing had to go from the eighth floor of the Business Center to the parking spot outside the first-floor entrance. Therefore, the route from the eighth floor of the Business Center to the parking spot was a necessary area for Sun Lixing to travel between the two workplaces and should be considered part of the workplace. The Park Labor Bureau's determination that the location where Sun Lixing fell was not his workplace, thereby excluding the necessary route for completing the work task from the workplace, was not only inconsistent with the legislative intent but also contrary to common sense. Sun Lixing's fall from the Zhongli Company office on the eighth floor of the Business Center to the first floor and on the steps at the first-floor entrance was caused by his need to complete the work task of driving to pick someone up. The appellant, the Park Labor Bureau, argued that Sun Lixing was not injured while driving and therefore not injured "due to work-related reasons," but this argument was untenable. Accordingly, the court revoked the "Decision on Work-related Injury Identification" made by the Park Labor Bureau, the defendant, and ordered it to make a new specific administrative act within 60 days after the judgment took effect.

Case 3    He Peixiang v. Jiangsu Xinyi City Labor and Social Security Bureau — administrative dispute over work-related injury identification

— Regarding the determination of "on the way to and from work"

Basic Facts

The plaintiff, He Peixiang, was a teacher at the former Beigou Town Shijian Primary School. On the morning of December 22, 2006, the plaintiff was assigned by Shijian Primary School to attend a lecture at Xinyi West City Primary School and had lunch in Xinyi city center. Since there was no direct bus from Shijian Primary School and the plaintiff's residence to West City Primary School, the plaintiff traveled by a combination of motorcycle, bus, and walking. At around 15:40, when Xing Hanmin, He Jiqiang, Zhou Enyu, and others from Shijian Primary School were driving past the cement road at Dachenzhuang, Shijian Village, they found He Peixiang had fallen off his motorcycle on the cement road approximately 200 to 300 meters from Shijian Primary School, and he was immediately sent to the hospital for emergency treatment. On December 27, the plaintiff's unit filed an application for work-related injury identification with the defendant, the Jiangsu Xinyi City Labor and Social Security Bureau, regarding this injury, but later withdrew the application for some reason. In June 2007, the plaintiff directly filed an application for work-related injury identification with the defendant regarding this injury. After two rounds of work-related injury identification, two rounds of administrative reconsideration, and two rounds of litigation, the defendant issued a "Worker's Work-related Injury Identification" on December 26, 2009, determining that although the motor vehicle accident injury suffered by He Peixiang occurred on a reasonable route to and from work, it did not occur within a reasonable time for commuting, and thus was not in the course of commuting and not identified as a work-related injury. The plaintiff refused to accept this and applied for administrative reconsideration to the Xinyi City People's Government. The reconsideration authority issued a decision upholding the defendant's work-related injury identification. Thereafter, the plaintiff filed a lawsuit with the court, requesting the revocation of the defendant's work-related injury identification.

Judgment

After trial at first instance by the Jiangsu Xinyi City People's Court and at second instance by the Xuzhou Intermediate People's Court, the court held that "reasonable time" and "reasonable route" in the context of "on the way to and from work" are two interrelated spatiotemporal concepts essential for determining whether an injury caused by a motor vehicle accident occurred during the commute and should not be separated. In this case, He Peixiang fell and injured himself while riding a motorcycle on his way back to school after attending the morning lecture and having lunch. His purpose in returning to school for work was clear, and this should be considered a reasonable time. Accordingly, the court revoked the "Worker's Work-related Injury Identification" made by the defendant, Xinyi City Labor and Social Security Bureau, and ordered the defendant to make a new decision regarding He Peixiang's application for work-related injury identification within sixty days from the date the judgment took effect.

Case 4    Zou Zhengxian v. Guangdong Foshan Chancheng District Labor and Social Security Bureau — administrative dispute over work-related injury identification

— Where the time limit for applying for work-related injury identification is exceeded for reasons not attributable to the employee or their close relatives, the time so delayed shall not be counted within the application period.

Basic Facts

Hongdahao Textile Company was a legally registered enterprise legal person, with its domicile within the jurisdiction of the defendant, the Guangdong Foshan Chancheng District Labor and Social Security Bureau. Deng Shangyan had a de facto labor relationship with Hongdahao Textile Company. On April 24, 2006, while operating a machine at an additional business premises unauthorizedly added by Hongdahao Textile Company, Deng Shangyan's left middle finger was crushed by the machine, diagnosed by the hospital as "closed fracture of the middle phalanx of the left middle finger, soft tissue contusion, and extensor tendon rupture." On July 28, without being aware of the circumstances, Deng Shangyan applied to the defendant for work-related injury identification, listing "Hongdahao Textile Factory" as the employing unit. The defendant rejected the application on the grounds that "Hongdahao Textile Factory" did not have the qualification of an employing entity and could not form a labor relationship with the worker. Deng Shangyan subsequently, through civil litigation, ultimately confirmed that the employing unit with which she had a de facto labor relationship was Hongdahao Textile Company. On January 16, 2008, Deng Shangyan applied to the defendant for work-related injury identification with Hongdahao Textile Company as the employing unit. The defendant issued a "Decision on Work-related Injury Identification" on January 28, determining that the injury suffered by Deng Shangyan on April 24, 2006, was a work-related injury. On March 24, 2008, Hongdahao Textile Company was approved for cancellation of registration by the administrative authority for industry and commerce. After Zou Zhengxian, as the former legal representative of Hongdahao Textile Company, received the "Decision on Work-related Injury Identification" on March 10, 2009, he refused to accept it and applied for administrative reconsideration to the Foshan City Labor and Social Security Bureau, which upheld the work-related injury identification. Zou Zhengxian still refused to accept this and filed an administrative lawsuit with the Foshan Chancheng District People's Court. The Chancheng District People's Court of Foshan, Guangdong Province, ruled to uphold the "Decision on Work-related Injury Identification" made by the defendant. After the judgment was pronounced, Zou Zhengxian refused to accept it and appealed to the Foshan Intermediate People's Court of Guangdong Province.

Judgment

The court, after trial, held that because Hongdahao Textile Company had unauthorizedly added business premises to conduct operations without legal registration, Deng Shangyan did not have subjective fault when she mistakenly listed "Hongdahao Textile Factory" as the employing unit in her application for work-related injury identification on July 28, 2006, being unaware of the true circumstances. Furthermore, it was only after the Chancheng Labor Bureau rejected Deng Shangyan's work-related injury identification application on the grounds that "Hongdahao Textile Factory" lacked employing entity qualifications and could not form a labor relationship with the worker, and suggested that Deng Shangyan resolve the issue through civil litigation, that the final civil judgment confirmed that the employing unit with which she had a de facto labor relationship was Hongdahao Textile Company. Therefore, after receiving Deng Shangyan's application for work-related injury identification on January 16, 2008, with Hongdahao Textile Company as the employing unit, the Chancheng Labor Bureau, considering the legislative purpose of the Regulations on Work-related Injury Insurance to effectively protect the legitimate rights and interests of workers, determined that Deng Shangyan had already filed an application for work-related injury identification within the one-year statutory limitation period. The delay in preserving her legitimate rights was due to reasons not attributable to her. Therefore, accepting her application and issuing an identification of work-related injury was procedurally proper. The defendant's application of law based on the established facts was correct. In accordance with the provisions of the Administrative Procedure Law, the court upheld the "Decision on Work-related Injury Identification" made by the defendant.
